name: Amos
author: The book is named after Amos, a man from Tekoa, a small village in the hill country of Judah, a few miles south of Bethlehem. He was not a professional prophet or a priest; he worked as a herdsman of sheep and also tended sycamore-fig trees. He travelled north to deliver his messages in the neighbouring kingdom of Israel. Most scholars accept that the core of the book comes from Amos himself, though many think some passages were added or arranged later by those who preserved his words.
audience: His first hearers were the people of the northern kingdom of Israel, especially the wealthy in the capital, Samaria, and worshippers at the royal shrine of Bethel. They were living through a time of peace and prosperity, busy with festivals and offerings, while a sharp gap had opened between rich landowners and the poor.
era: Amos spoke around 760–750 BC, when Uzziah ruled Judah in the south and Jeroboam II ruled Israel in the north. With the great empire of Assyria (in what is now Iraq) temporarily weakened, Jeroboam had won back territory and trade flourished, bringing fine houses and luxury goods to the upper classes. Within a few decades Assyria grew strong again, and in 722 BC it destroyed Samaria and ended the northern kingdom.

notes.1:1: Amos is dated 'two years before the earthquake'; a major earthquake in Uzziah's reign was remembered for generations, and archaeologists find signs of one around 760 BC.
notes.1:3: Damascus was the capital of Aram (roughly modern Syria), which had fought Israel for years over Gilead, the farmland east of the Jordan River.
notes.1:6: Gaza was one of the main Philistine cities on the Mediterranean coast, south-west of Judah.
notes.1:9: Tyre was a wealthy Phoenician port on the coast north of Israel, famous for its sea trade.
notes.1:11: Edom lay south-east of the Dead Sea; its people were traditionally descended from Esau, Jacob's brother, and had a long history of conflict with Israel.
notes.1:13: Ammon lay east of the Jordan, around today's Amman, and competed with Israel for control of Gilead.
notes.2:1: Moab was the kingdom east of the Dead Sea, a frequent neighbour and rival of both Israel and Edom.
notes.2:4: Judah was the southern kingdom, centred on Jerusalem, and Amos's own homeland.
notes.2:6: Here Amos turns to the northern kingdom of Israel itself, the very people he had come to address.
notes.3:9: Samaria, Israel's hilltop capital, had grand houses; archaeologists there have found carved ivory panels like the ivory-decorated homes mentioned in this passage.
notes.4:1: Bashan was rich pastureland east of the Jordan known for well-fed cattle; the words are aimed at wealthy women of Samaria.
notes.4:4: Bethel and Gilgal were the best-known worship sites in northern Israel; Bethel had been a royal shrine since the kingdom split around 930 BC.
notes.5:4: Beersheba, a pilgrimage site in the far south of Judah, drew worshippers from the north as well as Bethel and Gilgal.
notes.5:18: People in Amos's day looked forward to 'the day of the Lord', a time they expected God to step in and defeat Israel's enemies.
notes.6:1: Calneh and Hamath in Syria and the Philistine city of Gath were places Amos's hearers knew had already been conquered or humbled.
notes.6:8: Lo-debar and Karnaim were towns east of the Jordan captured in Jeroboam II's campaigns, which had pushed Israel's borders north toward Hamath.
notes.7:1: The 'king's mowing' probably refers to the first cut of hay taken for the royal herds, before the farmers' own spring crop grew.
notes.8:4: Trade stopped on the new moon festival and the Sabbath; merchants measured grain by the ephah, a dry measure, and weighed silver in shekels.
notes.8:9: A total eclipse of the sun was visible in this region in 763 BC, and some scholars think it was fresh in people's memories.
notes.8:11: Dan, in the far north, was another royal shrine, set up alongside Bethel when the kingdom divided.
notes.9:1: The altar in this vision is usually understood to be the one at Bethel, the shrine where Amos had preached.
notes.9:7: Cush was the land south of Egypt; Caphtor is usually identified with Crete, the Philistines' homeland; Kir was the Arameans' place of origin.
notes.9:11: Many scholars think this hopeful ending was added after Jerusalem fell in 586 BC; others hold that it comes from Amos himself.

flags.problem: The phrase 'two years before the earthquake' is a direct quotation from the verse, and the rules forbid quoting scripture.
flags.suggestion: Paraphrase it: 'The book dates Amos's preaching to two years before a famous earthquake; a major earthquake in Uzziah's reign was remembered for generations, and archaeologists find signs of one around 760 BC.'

flags.problem: The wording is confusing. 'Drew worshippers from the north as well as Bethel and Gilgal' reads as if Bethel and Gilgal sent worshippers to Beersheba. The intended point is that northerners went to Beersheba as well as to Bethel and Gilgal. Beersheba is also named in 5:5, not 5:4.
flags.suggestion: Move the note to 5:5 and reword: 'Beersheba, a pilgrimage site in the far south of Judah, drew worshippers from the north, who travelled there as well as to Bethel and Gilgal.'

flags.problem: It is stated as settled fact that the hearers already knew Calneh, Hamath and Gath as conquered. Scholars disagree. Some link these defeats to earlier events, such as Aramean attacks or Uzziah's campaign against Gath. Others link them to Assyrian conquests after 740 BC, which would make the verse a later addition. The places are also named in 6:2, not 6:1.
flags.suggestion: Move the note to 6:2 and add a short clause: 'Calneh and Hamath in Syria and the Philistine city of Gath were cities that had suffered defeat; some scholars think this refers to setbacks before Amos's time, others to Assyrian conquests a few decades later.'

flags.problem: Lo-debar and Karnaim are mentioned in 6:13, not 6:8, so the note is attached to the wrong verse.
flags.suggestion: Move the note to 6:13. If you want to cover the reference to Hamath, place that part at 6:14.

flags.problem: The claim is doubtful. The eclipse of 763 BC was total along a path through northern Mesopotamia (Assyria). In Israel it would have been only a deep partial eclipse.
flags.suggestion: Reword: 'A major eclipse of the sun in 763 BC, total in Assyria and clearly visible across the region, may have been fresh in people's memories, some scholars think.'

flags.problem: Dan is mentioned in 8:14, not 8:11, so the note is attached to the wrong verse.
